label: 1 Peter 1:1
text:
"Apostle" is apostolos, the word for a formally commissioned envoy, not a self-appointed volunteer — Peter opens by staking his authority to write on the office itself.

"Strangers" translates parepidēmois, a rarer and more specific word than the ordinary term for a foreigner: it names someone residing temporarily in a land not their own, present but never settled, always due to move on.

"Scattered" is diasporas — the same word Judaism used for the dispersion of Jews outside Palestine — and Peter reaches for it deliberately, casting these mostly Gentile believers as the true, spiritual Israel now scattered through the nations.

The five regions named cover the whole of Roman Asia Minor, listed roughly in the order a courier carrying this letter would have traveled them.
translation: Peter, an emissary of Jesus Christ, to the temporarily-residing exiles of the dispersion of Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia,

label: 1 Peter 1:2
text:
"Foreknowledge" is prognōsin — not bare advance information but a knowing that is relational and purposive, the same root sense as "to know" a spouse; God's foreknowing already includes his choosing love.

"Sanctification" is hagiasmos, naming an ongoing action rather than a finished state — the Spirit's continuous work of setting a person apart, not a one-time declaration.

"Unto obedience" governs both halves that follow: obedience to Christ and the sprinkling of his blood name the same reality from two sides — the position secured at the cross and the practice that position produces.

"Sprinkling" (rhantismon) deliberately echoes Exodus 24, where Moses sprinkled blood on the people to ratify the covenant at Sinai; Peter is telling scattered believers they stand inside a new, blood-ratified covenant.

"Multiplied" is plēthyntheiē, an optative of wish — not a flat statement that grace and peace exist, but a prayer that they increase exponentially, spread out further and further.
translation: According to the foreknowledge of God the Father, in sanctification of the Spirit, unto obedience and the sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ: may grace be multiplied to you, and peace.

label: 1 Peter 1:3
text:
"Blessed" is eulogētos, a word reserved in the New Testament for God alone — never used of a human being, unlike the related eulogēmenos.

"Abundant mercy" renders polu autou eleos, literally "his much mercy" — Peter piles the adjective on the noun rather than qualifying the verb, making mercy itself the thing measured as vast.

"Begotten us again" is anagennaō, a rare compound Peter is one of the only writers to use — not John's more familiar "born from above," but specifically a re-begetting, a second fathering that produces an entirely new kind of life.

"Lively hope" is elpida zōsan, "a living hope" — hope treated as an active, breathing thing rather than a static feeling, and it is alive specifically because it is generated dia ("through") the resurrection, not merely inspired by it.
translation: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his great mercy has begotten us again unto a living hope, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ out from among the dead,

label: 1 Peter 1:4
text:
Three alpha-privative adjectives stack up in a row, each negating a different way an inheritance decays: aphtharton, "incorruptible" — not subject to inward decomposition; amianton, "undefiled" — never touched or stained from outside; amaranton, "unfading" — never wilting with age, the word later giving us "amaranth," a flower legendary for never withering.

"Reserved" is tetērēmenēn, a perfect passive participle — the inheritance was placed in safekeeping at some point already past, and it continues, right now, to be kept that way; the guarding is not future but presently in force.
translation: Unto an inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled, and unfading, having been kept — and continuing to be kept — in the heavens for you,

label: 1 Peter 1:5
text:
Where the inheritance is kept (tēreō, verse 4), the heirs themselves are phrouroumenous, "garrisoned" — a military term for troops posted to guard a fortress, the same word Paul uses for the peace of God standing sentry over the heart in Philippians 4:7.

The verb is present tense: not a single past act of protection but a continuous, standing guard, actively maintained around believers right now.

"Ready to be revealed" translates a verb and adjective both looking toward a fixed, already-scheduled moment — the salvation isn't being assembled or decided; it is finished and simply waiting for its unveiling.
translation: Who are being garrisoned by the power of God, through faith, unto a salvation ready to be revealed in the last time.

label: 1 Peter 1:6
text:
"Greatly rejoice" is agalliasthe, an intensive, exuberant word for joy — stronger and more demonstrative than the ordinary chairō, closer to leaping or exulting out loud.

"For a season" is oligon, "a little," modifying not the trials' intensity but their duration — whatever their weight, Peter insists on their brevity against the horizon of verse 5's coming salvation.

"If need be" (ei deon) concedes that the grieving is sometimes genuinely necessary, not merely permitted — real sorrow, honestly felt, within a joy that still holds.

"Manifold" is poikilois, literally "many-colored, variegated" — the same adjective used elsewhere of the many-sided grace of God (4:10); the trials come in as many different shades as the grace that meets them.
translation: In which you exult, though now, for a little while, if it is necessary, you have been grieved by various trials,

label: 1 Peter 1:7
text:
"Trial" is to dokimion, naming not the test itself but the tested, approved quality that survives it — the same word used in the Septuagint for the assaying of precious metal.

Faith is set in explicit comparison with gold, and found "much more precious" (polytimoteron) — gold, for all its value, still perishes; approved faith does not.

"Tried with fire" (dia pyros dokimazomenou) is present tense, describing gold currently undergoing assay even as Peter writes the sentence — faith's testing is pictured as an ongoing smelting, not a single past ordeal.

The threefold "praise and honour and glory" piles up three separate words for a single moment of vindication — approval expressed, standing conferred, and radiance bestowed, all released together at Christ's unveiling.
translation: So that the proven genuineness of your faith — much more precious than gold that perishes, though it is being tested by fire — may be found unto praise and honor and glory at the unveiling of Jesus Christ,

label: 1 Peter 1:8
text:
Two participles run in tight parallel and contrast — "not having seen" (ouk idontes, aorist) against "now not seeing" (mē horōntes, present) — Peter distinguishes a past absence of any sighting from a present, ongoing absence of sight, and love and belief cross both without needing either.

"Unspeakable" is aneklalētō, a word apparently coined for this very passage — not found elsewhere in Greek before Peter uses it — joy too large for language to carry.

"Full of glory" is dedoxasmenē, a perfect passive participle — glory is not merely anticipated in the joy but already deposited there, a joy already glorified in advance of the glory it awaits.
translation: Whom, not having seen, you love; in whom, though now not seeing him, but believing, you exult with joy unspeakable and already glorified,

label: 1 Peter 1:9
text:
"Receiving" is komizomenoi, a middle-voice participle meaning to carry off for oneself, to obtain as one's own possession or reward — not a gift merely handed over but a prize actively secured and taken home.

"The end" is to telos — the intended goal or outcome a process was always aimed at, not its termination; faith was never open-ended, it was always headed somewhere.

That goal, "the salvation of your souls," is present tense in the Greek even in a sentence about a future unveiling — a salvation already being received, in the soul, even while its full disclosure still lies ahead.
translation: Obtaining for yourselves the outcome of your faith: the salvation of your souls.

label: 1 Peter 1:10–12
text:
"Searched diligently" and "searched" render two different, both intensive, compound verbs — exezētēsan and exēraunēsan — each built on a root for careful investigation with the intensifying ex- prefix bolted on: not a passing curiosity but a thorough, exhaustive digging.

"The Spirit of Christ" already active in Old Testament prophets asserts, in passing, Christ's personal preexistence — the Spirit who spoke through Isaiah and the Psalms is identified as belonging to the Christ not yet born.

The prophets searched for "what manner of time" (poion kairon) — poios asking after quality and character, not calendar dates: not merely when the Messiah would suffer, but what sort of season it would be, what shape the times would take.

"Look into" (parakypsai) pictures a bent, straining posture — the same verb used of Peter and John stooping to peer into the empty tomb — an intense angelic gaze bent forward to catch sight of something just out of full view.
translation: Concerning which salvation the prophets, who prophesied concerning the grace destined for you, sought out and searched out with care, searching into what person or what manner of time the Spirit of Christ within them was pointing to, as it testified beforehand the sufferings destined for Christ, and the glories after these things; to whom it was revealed that not to themselves, but to you, they were ministering the things which now have been announced to you by those who preached the good news to you by the Holy Spirit sent from heaven — things into which angels long to stoop down and look.

label: 1 Peter 1:13
text:
"Gird up" translates anazōsamenoi, the picture of a robed man reaching down to tuck the loose hem of his garment into his belt before running or working — mental preparation pictured as physical readiness for exertion.

"Loins" stands for the seat of thought, the place from which decisions and intentions issue — the mind's freedom of movement is what needs tucking up and unencumbering.

"Be sober" is nēphontes, the ordinary word for staying clear of intoxication, applied here to clarity of mind rather than abstinence from wine — undistracted, unclouded thinking.

"To the end" is teleiōs, "perfectly, completely" — the hope in view is not a partial or occasional confidence but one held all the way through, without qualification.
translation: Therefore, having girded up the loins of your mind, being sober, set your hope completely on the grace being brought to you at the unveiling of Jesus Christ.

label: 1 Peter 1:14–16
text:
"Fashioning yourselves" is syschēmatizomenoi, built on schēma, the outward form or pattern something is pressed into — the same verb Paul uses in Romans 12:2 for not being conformed to this age; the shape in view is external and temporary, not an inner nature.

"Ignorance" (agnoia) names the old life before knowledge of God arrived, and the "lusts" belonging to it are described as simply its natural byproduct — the desires a mind without God inevitably produces.

"As he which hath called you is holy" grounds the command in the caller's own character rather than in a rule external to him — holiness is required because it already belongs to the one who did the calling.

Peter quotes Leviticus (11:44; 19:2) almost word for word, taking a command originally addressed to Israel's ceremonial separateness and applying it directly to this scattered, largely Gentile readership — extending Israel's vocation onto the church.
translation: As children of obedience, not fashioning yourselves according to the former lusts, in your ignorance, but according to the Holy One who called you, be yourselves also holy in all your conduct; because it stands written: Be holy, because I am holy.

label: 1 Peter 1:17
text:
"Without respect of persons" is aprosōpolēptōs, a compound built on "face" and "receive" — literally "not face-receiving," refusing to judge by outward appearance or rank; Peter applies to God's courtroom the very fairness he demands of human judges elsewhere in the letter.

"Judgeth" is present tense, naming an ongoing, continuous activity of evaluation, not a single future assize — the Father is described as one presently, habitually weighing every man's work.

"Sojourning" is paroikias, the noun form of the same root behind "strangers" in verse 1 — the time of temporary, foreign residence, framed here explicitly as something to be passed "in fear," not in the comfort of a permanent home.
translation: And if you call upon him as Father, who without partiality judges according to each one's work, conduct yourselves in fear during the time of your temporary residence,

label: 1 Peter 1:18–19
text:
"Redeemed" is elutrōthēte, drawn from lytron, the ransom price paid to free a slave or captive — the verb assumes a real transaction, a price actually paid, not a metaphor for release without cost.

"Corruptible things" and "silver and gold" are dismissed together as inadequate currency — Peter names the single most valuable payment the ancient world knew, precisely in order to declare it insufficient.

"Vain conversation received by tradition from your fathers" (mataias anastrophēs patroparadotou) describes an entire inherited way of life, handed down father to son, as empty — futile in the sense of producing nothing of lasting worth.

"Without blemish and without spot" (amōmou kai aspilou) are sacrificial terms, the vocabulary of Levitical inspection for an offering fit to be presented — applied here to Christ himself as the qualifying, examined Lamb.
translation: Knowing that you were redeemed from your futile way of life handed down from your fathers, not with perishable things, silver or gold, but with precious blood, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot, the blood of Christ,

label: 1 Peter 1:20–21
text:
"Foreordained" is proegnōsmenou, literally "foreknown" — the same root as prognōsin in verse 2, tying the Father's foreknowledge of believers to his prior knowledge of the Son's appointed role; both are the same eternal purpose viewed from two angles.

"Before the foundation of the world" places that foreknowledge outside of time altogether, prior to creation itself, while "manifest" (ephanerōthē) marks the Incarnation as a specific, datable event within it — an eternal plan stepping into history "in these last times."

"For you" (di' hymas) insists the timing of that manifestation was calculated with this generation specifically in view, not merely an arbitrary point on a timeline.

"That your faith and hope might be in God" makes the entire chain — foreknowledge, manifestation, resurrection, glory — instrumental to one final aim: settling the believer's confidence squarely on God himself, not on Christ's work considered in isolation.
translation: Who was foreknown indeed before the foundation of the world, but was manifested in these last times for your sake, who through him believe in God, who raised him out from among the dead and gave him glory, so that your faith and hope might be fixed on God.

label: 1 Peter 1:22
text:
"Purified" is hēgnikotes, a perfect participle — a cleansing already accomplished and still standing in effect, achieved specifically "in obeying the truth," making obedience itself the instrument of the purifying.

"Unfeigned" is anypokriton, built on the same root as "hypocrite" with the alpha of negation prefixed — love with no actor's mask on it, nothing performed for an audience.

"Fervently" is ektenōs, literally "stretched out" — the picture of a muscle or rope pulled taut to its fullest extension, describing love given at full, straining intensity rather than a comfortable minimum.

"Pure heart" (katharas kardias) sets the standard for that love's origin — not merely its outward performance but the unmixed motive it must spring from.
translation: Having purified your souls in the obedience of the truth unto unfeigned brotherly love, love one another fervently, from a pure heart,

label: 1 Peter 1:23
text:
"Born again" repeats anagennaō from verse 3, and Peter immediately specifies its means: not "of corruptible seed" (ek sporas phthartēs) — human generation, which produces only more mortal life — but "of incorruptible" (aphthartou), a seed that carries its own imperishability into what it produces.

That incorruptible seed is then identified as "the word of God," described with two present participles, zōntos and menontos — "living" and "abiding" — not a word that once lived and spoke but one presently alive and presently remaining in force, continuously generative.
translation: Having been begotten again, not of corruptible seed, but of incorruptible, through the word of God, which is living and abiding.

label: 1 Peter 1:24–25
text:
Peter quotes Isaiah 40:6-8 almost verbatim, setting "all flesh" (pasa sarx) — every merely human existence and everything it produces, including "the glory of man" — against the single, unfading "word of the Lord."

"Withereth" and "falleth away" are both aorist, the tense the Septuagint uses for a general, timeless truth — this is not describing one flower's fate but the fixed pattern every human flourishing follows, without exception.

"Endureth for ever" closes the contrast in the present tense, and the final clause identifies that enduring word directly with "the word which by the gospel is preached unto you" — the very message these scattered believers received is, Peter insists, the one thing in the passage that does not fade.
translation: Because all flesh is like grass, and all its glory like the flower of grass; the grass withers, and the flower falls off, but the word of the Lord remains forever. And this is the word which was proclaimed as good news to you.

label: 1 Peter 2:1–3
text:
"Laying aside" is apothemenoi, aorist — a decisive, once-for-all stripping off, the picture of taking off a garment, not a gradual fading.

"Guile" (dolon) is literally bait — the word for what lures a fish onto a hook — making the whole list a catalogue of ways people are caught and used rather than loved.

"Newborn babes" is artigennēta brephē: arti means "just now, this very moment," and brephos can mean an infant still in the womb — the most recently begotten life imaginable, still gasping its first breath.

"Sincere" is adolon, the same root as "guile" (dolon) in verse 1 with the alpha of negation attached — deliberately: the milk that feeds this new life must be exactly what the old life's speech was told to put away.

"Of the word" is logikon, "belonging to reason, to the logos" — not milk about the word merely, but milk that is itself reasonable, rational, fitted to a mind now capable of feeding on truth.

"Gracious" is chrēstos — good, kind, useful — chosen for its near-identical sound to "Christos"; Peter's readers would have heard the pun even reading silently.
translation: Therefore, having put off all malice, and all guile, and hypocrisies, and envies, and all evil speakings, as newborn babes, long for the guileless milk of the word, so that by it you may grow up unto salvation, if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is good.

label: 1 Peter 2:4–5
text:
"Coming" is proserchomenoi, present tense — not a single approach already completed but a continuous, ongoing drawing near, repeated again and again.

"Disallowed" is apodedokimasmenon, a perfect passive participle: tested by men and permanently rejected — the same dokim- root that named faith's approved genuineness in 1:7, here applied to a verdict that turned out wrong.

"Living stone" fuses two categories that don't naturally belong together, stone and life, and Peter immediately does it again to his readers: "ye also, as lively stones" — the same paradox extended from Christ to the church built on him.

"Built up" (oikodomeisthe) is a form that can be read either as a statement, "you are being built," or a command, "be built up" — the ambiguity may be deliberate, describing something already happening that also demands cooperation.

"Spiritual sacrifices" reframes the whole of the old cultic system in non-material terms — a priesthood that offers nothing that can be seen or weighed, only what is acceptable "through Jesus Christ," the phrase that alone makes such offerings possible.
translation: To whom coming, a living stone, rejected indeed by men, but with God chosen and precious, you yourselves also, as living stones, are being built up a spiritual house, unto a holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.

label: 1 Peter 2:6–8
text:
"Chief corner stone" translates akrogōniaion, literally "highest-corner (stone)" — not a decorative capstone but the foundation stone set first, the one every other line and angle of the building is measured against.

"Confounded" is kataischynthē — put to open shame, publicly disgraced; the promise is not merely inward peace but the reversal of every public humiliation believers might presently be suffering.

Peter builds three Old Testament citations around a single word-family, dokim-: the stone once "disallowed" (apodokimazō) by human testers becomes, in God's testing, the very "head of the corner" — the same verb, opposite verdict.

"Stumbling" (proskommatos) and "offence" (skandalou) both trade on the same picture — skandalon originally named the trigger-stick of an animal trap — Christ becomes, for those who reject him, exactly the trap-mechanism that catches them.

"Being disobedient" identifies the object of "whereunto also they were appointed" — it is their disobedience to the word, not their doom as such, that stands appointed; the stumbling is the fixed, foreknown consequence of a choice, not an arbitrary decree.
translation: Because it is contained in scripture: Behold, I lay in Zion a chosen, precious chief corner stone, and he who believes on him shall by no means be put to shame. To you, then, who believe belongs the preciousness; but to those who are disobedient, the stone which the builders rejected, this one has become the head of the corner, and a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense — to those who stumble at the word, being disobedient, unto which also they were appointed.

label: 1 Peter 2:9–10
text:
"Chosen generation" is genos eklekton — genos names a race, family, or kind, not merely a cohort born at the same time; Peter is naming a people bound by shared origin, not shared birth-year.

"Royal priesthood" and "holy nation" lift phrases directly from Exodus 19:6, where they first named Israel at Sinai — Peter transfers Israel's own covenant vocabulary onto this scattered, largely Gentile readership without qualification.

"Peculiar people" renders laos eis peripoiēsin, literally "a people unto possessing" — not people who are odd, but people acquired, purchased outright for God's own keeping.

"Shew forth" is exangeilēte, "to announce out, to proclaim abroad" — a public, outward-facing task, not private gratitude kept to oneself.

The double contrast — "not a people" become "the people of God," "not obtained mercy" now having "obtained mercy" — is lifted almost verbatim from Hosea, where it first described Israel's own restoration after judgment.
translation: But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God's own possession, so that you may proclaim abroad the excellencies of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light; who once were not a people, but now are the people of God; who had not been shown mercy, but now have been shown mercy.

label: 1 Peter 2:11–12
text:
"Strangers and pilgrims" combines paroikous and parepidēmous — the noun forms of 1:1's parepidēmois and 1:17's paroikias — Peter binds the letter's opening and its ethical instruction together with the same word-pair.

"War against" is strateuontai, a military verb for waging an active campaign — the fleshly lusts are pictured not as passive temptations but as an army on continuous offensive against the soul.

"Conversation" is anastrophē — conduct, a whole manner of life, never mere speech in Peter's vocabulary; "honest" (kalēn) means beautiful, noble, attractive to look at, not merely inoffensive.

"Behold" is epopteusantes, a term borrowed from the mystery religions for what an initiate witnesses at the climax of the rites — Gentile observers are pictured watching believers' conduct with the same rapt attention.

"Visitation" is episkopēs, built on the same root as "bishop" (episkopos, "overseer") — the day God comes to inspect is imagined as the day these same watching Gentiles are brought, themselves, under his oversight.
translation: Beloved, I urge you, as sojourners and temporary residents, to abstain from the fleshly lusts which wage war against the soul, keeping your conduct honorable among the Gentiles, so that in the matter in which they speak against you as evildoers, they may, from observing your good works, glorify God in the day of visitation.

label: 1 Peter 2:13–17
text:
"Submit yourselves" is hypotagēte, a military rank-term for taking one's assigned place under authority — voluntary self-positioning, not forced subjugation.

"Ordinance" translates ktisei, literally "creation" — Peter calls human government itself a kind of creation, a structure God has brought into being within the created order, however imperfectly men occupy it.

"Put to silence" is phimoun, "to muzzle" — the exact verb for fitting an animal with a muzzle; good conduct doesn't merely answer slander, it forcibly shuts the slanderer's mouth.

"Cloak" (epikalymma) names a covering used to hide something underneath — liberty is not to be worn as a costume disguising continued evil.

"Honour" (timēsate) is aorist imperative — a decisive act, done once and repeated — while "fear" (phobeisthe) is present imperative, continuous reverence reserved for God alone; Peter's grammar itself keeps the king's honor and God's fear from ever being the same thing.
translation: Submit yourselves to every human institution for the Lord's sake, whether to a king as supreme, or to governors as sent by him for the punishment of evildoers, and the praise of those who do good — because so is the will of God, that by doing good you silence the ignorance of foolish men — as free, and not holding your freedom as a covering for evil, but as bondslaves of God. Honor all men; love the brotherhood; continually fear God; honor the king.

label: 1 Peter 2:18–20
text:
"Servants" is oiketai, household servants specifically — a narrower, more intimate word than the general doulos, naming those who live inside the family's own home.

"Froward" is skoliois, literally "crooked, twisted" — the same root that gives medicine the word "scoliosis" for a curved spine; the master in view isn't merely difficult but bent out of true.

"Thankworthy" translates charis — literally "grace" — a striking choice: unjust suffering, endured for conscience' sake, is itself named an instance of grace, not merely something grace helps a person survive.

"Buffeted" is kolaphizomenoi, "struck with the fist" — the same verb used of the blows Jesus received before his crucifixion — deliberate, physical, humiliating violence, not abstract hardship.

The repeated question "what glory is it" measures the value of endurance strictly against its cause: suffering earned by wrongdoing carries no credit at all; only suffering for good, patiently borne, "is acceptable with God" (touto charis para theō).
translation: Household servants, be subject to your masters with all fear, not only to the good and gentle, but also to the crooked. For this is grace, if because of conscience toward God someone bears up under grief, suffering unjustly. For what credit is it, if when you sin and are beaten for it you endure it patiently? But if, when you do good and suffer for it, you endure it patiently, this is grace with God.

label: 1 Peter 2:21–25
text:
"Example" is hypogrammon, a schoolroom term for a copied writing-pattern set at the top of a page for children to trace letter by letter — Christ's suffering isn't offered as inspiration but as a stroke-for-stroke pattern to be retraced.

"Follow" (epakolouthēsēte) matches that image exactly — to follow closely upon, tracing the very line already laid down.

"Committed himself" is paredidou, imperfect tense — not a single decision made once but a continuous, repeated handing-over, sustained all through the ordeal of the trial and crucifixion.

"Bare" is anēnenken, sacrificial vocabulary for carrying an offering up to the altar — our sins are pictured as the very thing carried up and laid on the cross itself, described here in the Greek simply as xylon, "wood, tree," recalling the curse pronounced in Deuteronomy on anyone hanged on a tree.

"Stripes" is mōlōpi, singular — one collective wound or welt standing for the whole scourging, matching Isaiah's own singular "by his stripes we are healed."

"Bishop" is episkopon, "overseer, guardian" — the same root as "visitation" in 2:12 — sheep once scattered without direction are pictured returning not merely to a shepherd but to one who actively watches over them.
translation: For to this you were called, because Christ also suffered for you, leaving behind for you a copy to trace, so that you should follow closely upon his steps; who committed no sin, nor was guile found in his mouth; who, being reviled, did not revile in return; suffering, he kept on not threatening, but kept on committing himself to him who judges righteously; who himself carried up our sins in his own body onto the tree, so that, having died to sins, we might live to righteousness — by whose wound you were healed. For you were continually going astray like sheep, but have now turned back to the shepherd and overseer of your souls.

label: 1 Peter 3:1–2
text:
"In subjection" (hypotassomenai) is the same rank-term already used of citizens toward government (2:13) and servants toward masters (2:18) — Peter treats the wife's submission as one instance of a single, larger pattern running through the whole letter, not a category by itself.

"Won" is kerdēthēsontai, a commercial verb meaning "gained, profited" — the ordinary word for turning a business profit, applied here to a husband becoming a spiritual asset gained without a sale ever being pitched to him.

"Without the word" (aneu logou) is emphatic by position — not a single sermon preached, but conduct doing alone what speech is expressly barred from doing here.

"Behold" is epopteusantes again, the mystery-rite word from 2:12 — the husband is pictured as an initiate watching, rapt, something unfold in front of him that changes his mind without changing the subject of conversation.
translation: Likewise, wives, being submissive to your own husbands, so that even if some are disobedient to the word, they may, without a word, be won over through the conduct of their wives, observing your pure conduct joined with reverence.

label: 1 Peter 3:3–4
text:
"Adorning" is kosmos — the same word as "world, order," the underlying idea being arrangement, things put into proper display; Peter isn't forbidding order but relocating where the real ordering happens.

"Hidden man of the heart" (ho kryptos tēs kardias anthrōpos) names an entire inner person, concealed from outward view — the true site of value shifts from what can be seen to what cannot.

"Incorruptible" (aphtharton) repeats the same word-family already used of the inheritance (1:4) and the seed of the new birth (1:23) — this ornament belongs to the identical category of thing that does not decay.

"Meek" is praus, a gentleness that is strength held under control, not weakness — the word used elsewhere of a trained animal's bridled power; "quiet" (hēsychios) names an undisturbed tranquility, not mere silence.

"Great price" (polytelous) is a term for extravagant, costly expense — the very opposite of gold and fine clothing being, in God's reckoning, the truly expensive item.
translation: Whose adornment let it not be the outward — braiding of hair, and wearing of gold ornaments, or putting on of dresses — but the hidden person of the heart, in the incorruptible quality of a gentle and tranquil spirit, which is, before God, of great price.

label: 1 Peter 3:5–6
text:
"Trusted" is ēlpizon, imperfect tense — not a single act of confidence but a hope continuously, repeatedly maintained across an entire life, the ordinary posture of these women rather than an isolated decision.

"Obeyed" shifts to aorist, hypēkousen — one particular, completed act of obedience singled out as representative: Sarah calling Abraham "lord," pictured as the summary instance of a whole pattern of life.

"Amazement" is ptoēsin, a rare word for a sudden, fluttering panic — the image behind it is a bird startled into flight; the fearlessness in view is freedom from that kind of jolting terror, not mere outward calm.
translation: For in this manner formerly the holy women also, who were hoping in God, were adorning themselves, being submissive to their own husbands — as Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord — whose children you have become, doing good, and not fearing any sudden terror.

label: 1 Peter 3:7
text:
"Dwell with" is synoikountes, present participle — an ongoing, daily cohabitation, not a single act of marrying but the continuous shared life that follows it.

"According to knowledge" (kata gnōsin) demands understanding as the operating principle of that shared life — knowledge of the other person specifically, not knowledge in general.

"Weaker vessel" uses a comparative, asthenesterō — not "weak" outright but weaker relative to the husband in some particular respect, most naturally physical strength, and skeuos, "vessel," is the same word used elsewhere for any instrument set apart for a purpose.

"Heirs together" is synklēronomoi, "co-inheritors" — the very same inheritance named back in 1:4, held jointly and without distinction between husband and wife.

"Hindered" is enkoptesthai, originally a military term for cutting up a road to block an advancing enemy's path — mistreatment of a wife is pictured as a physical roadblock thrown up against a man's own prayers.
translation: Husbands, likewise, dwell together with them according to knowledge, assigning honor to the wife as to a weaker vessel, and as fellow heirs of the grace of life, so that your prayers may not be cut off.

label: 1 Peter 3:8–9
text:
"Of one mind" is homophrones, a compound built directly from "same" and "mind" — thinking in genuine unison, not merely agreeing to disagree peaceably.

"Having compassion" is sympatheis, the direct ancestor of the English "sympathy" — literally "suffering with," feeling another's pain as one's own rather than observing it from a distance.

"Pitiful" is eusplanchnoi, literally "good-bowelled" — ancient thought located the seat of compassion in the inward organs, so the word pictures a person whose very insides are moved with tenderness.

"Not rendering evil for evil" sets up a strict grammatical parallel — the identical structure for insult repaid with insult — before breaking it deliberately with "but contrariwise blessing," present participle: a continuous, repeated practice of blessing set directly against a symmetry the flesh finds natural.
translation: Finally, all of you being of one mind, sympathizing, loving as brothers, tenderhearted, humble-minded, not rendering evil for evil, or insult for insult, but on the contrary, continually blessing, because unto this you were called, so that you might inherit a blessing.

label: 1 Peter 3:10–12
text:
Peter quotes Psalm 34 almost verbatim, and its imperatives run in a chain of decisive, punctiliar (aorist) commands — pausatō ("let him stop"), ekklinatō ("let him turn away"), diōxatō ("let him pursue") — each naming a single, deliberate action rather than a vague disposition.

"Ensue" translates diōxatō, the same verb used elsewhere for hunting down or persecuting a person — peace, in this picture, must be chased with the same energy normally spent chasing an enemy.

"His ears are open" is a Hebrew idiom carried straight over into the Greek, picturing God's ear literally inclined, bent toward the sound of prayer.

"Face...against" (prosōpon epi) is the same idiom in reverse — God's face is pictured as physically set, turned to confront, those who do evil, the identical posture of attention aimed in the opposite direction.
translation: For he who wishes to love life and to see good days, let him stop his tongue from evil, and his lips from speaking deceit; and let him turn away from evil, and let him do good; let him seek peace, and let him pursue it. Because the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are turned toward their petition; but the face of the Lord is set against those who do evil.

label: 1 Peter 3:13–17
text:
"Sanctify" is hagiasate, aorist imperative — a decisive setting-apart of the Lord in the heart, done as a definite act, not a gradual feeling cultivated over time.

"Answer" is apologian, the standard word for a formal courtroom defense speech — the same root behind English "apologetics" — believers are pictured as perpetually on call to give a reasoned legal defense, not merely a personal testimony.

"A reason" (logon) reinforces the same courtroom picture — an account that can actually be given, structured and articulate, not a vague gesture at feeling.

"Meekness and fear" (prautētos kai phobou) qualify how that defense is delivered — the content may be a confident legal case, but the tone must carry no defensiveness or contempt.

"Falsely accuse" is epēreazontes, a verb for abusive threatening — the accusers' own conduct is named as insulting even before their charges are shown false, so that their eventual shame is set up as a foregone conclusion.
translation: And who is the one who will harm you, if you become zealous for what is good? But even if you should suffer because of righteousness, you are blessed. And do not fear their fear, nor be troubled, but sanctify Christ as Lord in your hearts, always ready to give a defense to everyone who asks you a reason concerning the hope in you, but with meekness and reverence, having a good conscience, so that in the very thing in which you are spoken against, those who abusively threaten your good conduct in Christ may be put to shame. Because it is better, if the will of God should so will it, to suffer for doing good rather than for doing evil.

label: 1 Peter 3:18–20
text:
"Quickened" is zōopoiētheis, "made alive" — set in exact grammatical parallel with "put to death," the same aorist passive construction covering both, flesh and spirit named as the two spheres in which each event took place.

"Preached" is ekēryxen, "proclaimed as a herald" — a public, official announcement, not private instruction; the content proclaimed to these "spirits" is left unspecified, generating the passage's long-running interpretive debate over whether it names fallen angelic beings or Noah's own generation reached through the Spirit at work in him.

"Waited" (apexedecheto) is imperfect, describing God's patience as something sustained and ongoing across the entire span "while the ark was being prepared" (kataskeuazomenēs, present passive) — construction and patience both pictured as continuing, side by side, for the whole long wait.

"By water" (di' hydatos) can be read two ways at once in the Greek — the water as the very thing the ark passed safely through, and, in the next verse, water as the ordinary element then repurposed as a saving instrument in baptism.
translation: Because Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, so that he might bring us to God, having been put to death in the flesh, but made alive in the spirit; in which also, having gone, he made proclamation to the spirits in prison, who were once disobedient, when the patience of God kept waiting, in the days of Noah, while an ark was being prepared, into which a few — that is, eight souls — were brought safely through water.

label: 1 Peter 3:21–22
text:
"Like figure" is antitypon, "antitype" — the technical term for the later fulfillment corresponding to an earlier pattern; the flood-water becomes the type, and baptism the antitype answering to it.

"Answer" here is eperōtēma, likely a technical legal or contractual term for a formal pledge or undertaking given in response to a question — not the removal of dirt but a good conscience's solemn pledge made toward God.

"By the resurrection" (di' anastaseōs) makes plain what actually saves in this picture — not the water's physical action at all, but the resurrection the water points toward and depends on entirely.

"Made subject" is hypotagentōn, the identical verb-root running through the whole letter's submission theme — wives, servants, citizens — here applied cosmically, to angels and authorities and powers themselves, all placed under the risen Christ.
translation: Which water, as a corresponding type, now also saves you — that is, baptism, not a putting away of the filth of the flesh, but the pledge of a good conscience toward God — through the resurrection of Jesus Christ, who is at the right hand of God, having gone into heaven, angels and authorities and powers having been made subject to him.

label: 1 Peter 4:1–2
text:
"Arm yourselves" is hoplisasthe, straightforward military vocabulary for equipping with weapons — a mindset that must be actively put on before the battle, not assumed automatically.

"Same mind" (tēn autēn ennoian) points back one sentence, to Christ's own resolve to suffer in the flesh — the very thought-pattern that carried him to the cross is what believers are told to arm themselves with.

"Hath ceased from sin" is pepautai, perfect tense — not an ongoing struggle but a settled, completed state: suffering in the flesh, taken as Christ took it, is pictured as having already broken sin's claim, the way physical death ends a person's further dealings with this present life.
translation: Christ, then, having suffered in the flesh, you also arm yourselves with the same thought — because he who has suffered in the flesh has been brought to a standstill with sin — so as to live the remaining time in the flesh no longer for the lusts of men, but for the will of God.

label: 1 Peter 4:3–6
text:
"Suffice" is arketos, "sufficient" — a dry, almost weary understatement: one lifetime already spent that way was, more than adequately, enough.

"Excess of riot" translates asōtias anachysin — anachysis, "a pouring out, a flood," describes the excess itself, while asōtia, the same root behind the prodigal son's "riotous living," names a life poured out past any hope of recovery.

"Think it strange" is xenizontai, built on xenos, "stranger, foreigner" — the very word already used of believers themselves in 1:1; onlookers are baffled precisely because the believer has become, in this one respect, a foreigner to what used to be native territory.

"Preached" (euēngelisthē) to "them that are dead" most naturally names those who heard the gospel while alive and have since died — judged, in the flesh, by the common verdict every human being faces, yet living now, in spirit, by God's own reckoning.
translation: Because sufficient is the time already past for having worked out the will of the Gentiles, having gone on in sensuality, lusts, drunkenness, carousings, drinking parties, and lawless idolatries — in which they are surprised that you do not run with them into the same flood of dissipation, blaspheming; who will give account to him who is ready to judge the living and the dead. Because for this reason the good news was proclaimed also to the dead, so that they might be judged according to men in the flesh, but might live according to God in the spirit.

label: 1 Peter 4:7–11
text:
"At hand" is ēngiken, perfect tense — has drawn near and, right now, remains near; not an event approaching from a distance but one already standing at the door.

"Sober" (sōphronēsate) and "watch" (nēpsate) pair clear-headed judgment with wakeful alertness, the same combination Peter reaches for again at 5:8 — a mind neither clouded nor asleep.

"Fervent" repeats ektenē, the "stretched taut" word already used of love in 1:22 — this charity, too, is pictured at full extension, not offered at a comfortable minimum.

"Hospitality" is philoxenoi, literally "stranger-loving" — built on the identical xenos root already flagged in verse 4 — believers who are themselves strangers in the world are told to specialize in loving strangers.

"Manifold grace" is poikilēs charitos, the same "many-colored" adjective already applied to trials in 1:6 — grace comes in as many varied forms as the sufferings it answers.

"Oracles" is logia, a solemn word for divinely authoritative utterances — speaking "as the oracles of God" sets an almost unbearably high bar for anyone teaching in the assembly.
translation: But the end of all things has drawn near; be of sound mind, then, and be sober-minded unto prayers. Before all things, keep on having fervent love among yourselves, because love covers a multitude of sins. Be hospitable to one another without grumbling. According as each one has received a gift, minister it to one another as good stewards of the varied grace of God. If anyone speaks, let it be as speaking oracles of God; if anyone ministers, let it be as ministering out of the strength which God supplies, so that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ, to whom belongs the glory and the dominion, forever and ever. Amen.

label: 1 Peter 4:12–14
text:
"Think it strange" (xenizesthe) and "strange thing" (xenou) both repeat the xenos wordplay of verse 4 a third time — suffering itself is not, contrary to first appearances, foreign territory for a people already called foreigners; it belongs to their citizenship rather than interrupting it.

"Fiery trial" is pyrōsei, a burning — the vocabulary of metal refined in a furnace, echoing 1:7's faith "tried with fire" — suffering pictured, once again, as a smelting process rather than mere misfortune.

"Partakers" is koinōneite, present tense — an ongoing, continuous partnership in Christ's own sufferings, not a single occasion of resemblance.

"Resteth" is anapauetai, present tense — a settled, continuous repose, the Spirit of glory pictured not as visiting briefly but as remaining, at rest, upon the one being reproached.
translation: Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery ordeal occurring among you, coming to you for a trial, as though a strange thing were happening to you; but to the degree that you are sharing the sufferings of Christ, keep on rejoicing, so that also at the revelation of his glory you may rejoice, exulting. If you are being reproached in the name of Christ, blessed are you, because the Spirit of glory, even the Spirit of God, is resting upon you.

label: 1 Peter 4:15–16
text:
"Busybody in other men's matters" translates allotriepiskopos, a rare compound apparently coined for this very sentence — allotrios, "belonging to another," fused onto episkopos, "overseer": literally, a self-appointed overseer of what belongs to someone else.

The word sits in a list alongside murderer and thief with no softening — meddling in others' affairs is placed on the same moral footing as violent crime.

"As a Christian" (hōs Christianos) uses a term barely established when Peter writes it — likely first coined by outsiders as mockery (Acts 11:26) — and Peter takes the very label meant to shame his readers and turns it, without alteration, into grounds for glorifying God.
translation: But let none of you suffer as a murderer, or thief, or evildoer, or as a meddler in the affairs of others; but if as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but let him glorify God in this name.

label: 1 Peter 4:17–19
text:
"Begin" (arxasthai) frames judgment as a process already underway rather than a future event only — starting, deliberately, at "the house of God" itself before it reaches anyone outside it.

"Scarcely" is molis, "with difficulty, barely" — the righteous man's salvation is pictured as attained only just, straining every resource available, making the ungodly's prospects the more sobering by comparison.

"Commit" is paratithesthōsan, banking vocabulary for depositing something valuable into safekeeping — the identical picture Paul reaches for describing what he has "committed" to Christ against the last day.

"Creator" (ktistē) is the only place in the whole New Testament this noun is used directly of God — his trustworthiness to keep a deposit rests specifically on his identity as the one who made it in the first place.
translation: Because the time has come for judgment to begin from the household of God; and if it begins first from us, what will be the outcome for those who disobey the good news of God? And if the righteous is scarcely being saved, where will the ungodly and sinner appear? So then, let those also who are suffering according to the will of God entrust their souls, in well-doing, to a faithful Creator.

label: 1 Peter 5:1–4
text:
"Feed" is poimanate, the verb built directly on poimēn, "shepherd" — a task far broader than dispensing food, covering the entire range of pastoral care a shepherd owes a flock.

"Taking the oversight" is episkopountes, the same episkop- root already applied to God's own "visitation" (2:12) and to Christ as "Bishop of your souls" (2:25) — elders are pictured exercising, in miniature and under Christ, the identical oversight that belongs supremely to him.

"Filthy lucre" is aischrokerdōs, "shameful gain" — built on the same kerdos ("gain, profit") already used of a husband being "won" in 3:1, here turned to a shameful, mercenary use of ministry instead.

"Lords over" is katakyrieuontes, an intensive, compound form of "lord" describing harsh, domineering control — set against klērōn, "allotted portions," reminding elders that each flock is a charge assigned to them, never a private possession.

"Chief Shepherd" is archipoimenos, a rare compound coined to distinguish the one supreme Shepherd from the many under-shepherds just addressed — their crown, unlike theirs, is described as amarantinon, "amaranth-like," built on the same unfading root as the inheritance of 1:4.
translation: The elders among you I exhort, as a fellow elder and witness of the sufferings of Christ, and also a sharer of the glory about to be revealed: shepherd the flock of God among you, exercising oversight not under compulsion, but willingly, according to God; not for shameful gain, but eagerly; not as lording it over your allotted charges, but becoming examples to the flock. And when the Chief Shepherd is manifested, you will receive the unfading crown of glory.

label: 1 Peter 5:5–7
text:
"Clothed" is egkombōsasthe, a rare and vivid verb built on kombos, "a knot" — the precise picture is tying on a servant's work-apron over one's clothes; humility is imagined as a specific, menial garment deliberately knotted into place, not a general attitude.

"Resisteth" is antitassetai, a military term for taking up battle formation directly against an opposing army — God is pictured actively arrayed for combat against the proud, not merely disapproving of them.

"Mighty hand" (krataian cheira) echoes the exact Old Testament phrase for God's hand delivering Israel from Egypt — the same sovereign strength now applied to a believer's present humbling.

"Casting" is epiripsantes, aorist — a single, decisive throw, not an ongoing struggle to keep letting go; the anxiety is hurled once, bodily, onto someone else entirely.

"Careth for" is melei, present tense — it is, continuously and right now, a genuine concern to him, not a promise deferred to some future attention.
translation: Likewise, younger men, be submissive to the elders; and all of you tie on humility toward one another, because God arrays himself against the proud, but gives grace to the humble. Be humbled, then, under the mighty hand of God, so that he may exalt you at the proper time, having thrown all your anxiety upon him, because it is a care to him concerning you.

label: 1 Peter 5:8–9
text:
"Sober" and "vigilant" pair the same two verbs already joined at 1:13 and 4:7 — clear-headed judgment and wakeful alertness, the standing posture the letter keeps returning to.

"Adversary" is antidikos, a courtroom term for the opposing party in a lawsuit — the devil is pictured less as a monster in the shadows than as a litigant actively pressing a case.

"Roaring" is ōryomenos, the specific word for a lion's hunting roar, and "walketh about" (peripatei) is present tense — a continuous, restless prowling, not an occasional ambush.

"Resist" is antistēte, aorist imperative — a decisive stand taken at a given moment, while "stedfast" (stereoi) pictures that stand as solid, unyielding ground under the feet.

"Accomplished" is epiteleisthai, present passive — the identical sufferings are, right now, being carried out across the whole scattered brotherhood, so that no reader can imagine their own trial as an isolated, singular hardship.
translation: Be sober, be watchful; your adversary the devil walks about as a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour, whom resist, firm in the faith, knowing that the same sufferings are being accomplished in your brotherhood in the world.

label: 1 Peter 5:10–11
text:
"A while" (oligon) repeats the exact word already used of the trials in 1:6 — the suffering's brevity is measured, again, against the far larger scale of what follows it.

Four verbs stack up in a row, each a distinct metalworking or building image: katartisei, "to fully mend, equip" — the same word used of repairing torn fishing nets; stērixei, "to fix firmly in place"; sthenōsei, a rare verb meaning "to fill with strength"; themeliōsei, "to lay a foundation under."

Taken together, the four describe not one single action but the entire process of restoration — repaired, fixed, empowered, and founded — brought to bear on people who have only just finished suffering "a while."
translation: But the God of all grace, who called you to his eternal glory in Christ, after you have suffered a little while, will himself fully restore, fix firmly, fill with strength, and lay a foundation under you. To him be the dominion, forever and ever. Amen.

label: 1 Peter 5:12–14
text:
"Briefly" is di' oligōn, literally "through few (words)" — Peter frames the entire letter, however dense, as a short one by his own reckoning.

"Testifying" is epimartyrōn, an intensive compound of the ordinary verb "to witness" — a stronger, more solemn attesting than a simple statement of fact.

"Babylon" almost certainly functions as a coded name for Rome, following the same apocalyptic convention later used openly in Revelation — a scattered, persecuted readership would have caught the reference at once.

"Elected together with you" is syneklektē, a rare compound built on the same eklektos, "chosen," already applied to the readers themselves in 1:1 — the sister church in Rome is named, quite literally, "co-chosen" alongside them.

"Kiss of charity" (philēmati agapēs) names the customary greeting of the earliest church, agapē pressing the same word used throughout the letter for the highest, most deliberate kind of love into an ordinary physical gesture.
translation: Through Silvanus, our faithful brother, as I reckon, I have written to you briefly, exhorting and solemnly testifying this to be the true grace of God — stand fast in it. She who is co-chosen with you in Babylon greets you, and so does Mark, my son. Greet one another with a kiss of love. Peace to all of you who are in Christ.
